title: Punnika's question
hookLine: a water-carrier asks a brahmin: if bathing washed away evil, wouldn't the fish and frogs be saints? (Therigatha, Punnika)

cards: Why would anyone stand in a river in the cold if they didn't have to? Punnika has to.

She carries water for a household, and in her verses she says she goes down into the water in the cold, afraid of her mistresses' punishment. At the river she finds a brahmin, a priest, standing in the water, shivering.
She's there because she has to be. Why is he? So she asks him.

teach.b: First, her question. Brahmin, what are you afraid of, she asks, that you go down into the water with your limbs shaking in the cold? She knows what drives her.
She wonders what drives him. Second, his answer. He's doing good to undo evil, he says: whoever has done wrong, young or old, is freed of it by bathing.
Third, the frogs. Who told you that, she asks, someone who didn't know, telling someone else who didn't?
If water washed away wrongdoing, then the frogs and the turtles, the water snakes and the crocodiles would all go to heaven.

teach.h: THEN THE FROGS GO TO HEAVEN.
teach.b: And if the river carried off your wrongs, it would carry off your good deeds too, and leave you with nothing. Fourth, what she offers instead. If you fear suffering, she says, don't do harmful things, openly or in secret.

And she adds a kindness: don't let your body suffer in the cold. The brahmin is moved. He thanks her for turning him from the wrong road and takes refuge, and the poem ends with him saying that now he is truly washed.

teach.h: FROM THE SKIN TO THE DEEDS.
teach.b: The washing still matters; it has moved from the skin to the deeds.
This poem is one voice in an old conversation, told from inside the Buddha's community; in the Majjhima the Buddha makes a similar point about bathing in sacred rivers.
Hindus who bathe in holy rivers today speak for themselves about what that bathing means, and this poem doesn't speak for them.

how: Some Buddhist teachers read Punnika's verses as a teaching that purity comes from conduct and intention, and tell of a water-carrier whose plain question changed a priest's life.

o: a water-carrier asks why the brahmin bathes
a brahmin asks why she carries river water
a nun asks the Buddha if rivers are holy

games.q: Punnika at the river: tap the pairs.
p: would carry off good deeds too

s: Punnika goes down to the river because she wants to
she says she goes in the cold out of fear of her mistresses' punishment.
she says the river would wash away good deeds as well
if it carried off your wrongs, she says, it would carry off your good deeds too.
the poem ends with the brahmin angry and walking away
he thanks her and takes refuge, and the poem ends with him calling himself truly washed.

games.q: you're Punnika, carrying water in the cold. a brahmin is shivering in the river to wash away his wrongs. what do you do?
o: fill your jar and say nothing.
ask him what he's afraid of, and question his answer.
games.why: she asks, listens, and answers with the frogs and turtles. then she tells him to stop doing harm, and not to let his body suffer in the cold.

practice: Choose one thing you do by habit, small or large: a way you start the morning, a phrase you always say, a custom from your family or your faith. Ask it Punnika's question, plainly: what is this for?
You don't need to stop doing it, and sometimes the answer makes it richer; just ask, and listen for what comes back.

wordCard.voice: Punnika's question. A water-carrier asks a shivering brahmin why he bathes, and turns him from the river to the deeds themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali udaka: water. The brahmin trusts the water; Punnika points him to his deeds.

carryVoice: Your line: the frogs would be saints. A sharp question, asked with a kindness. Day seven hundred ninety-three, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 7 (Vatthupama Sutta: bathing in sacred rivers)
